sources.title: Outpatient treatment of COVID-19 and incidence of post-COVID-19 condition over 10 months (COVID-OUT): a multicentre, randomised, quadruple-blind, parallel-group, phase 3 trial
sources.population: Adults 30–85, overweight or obesity, acute COVID symptoms under 7 days; no known prior infection
sources.preview: Metformin started during acute infection was associated with fewer later clinician diagnoses in this randomized prevention trial. The result does not establish treatment benefit for people who already have long COVID. The long-term analysis used a selected follow-up group, and an identified correction still needs reconciliation. Read the outcome definition and newer trial evidence before treating the result as a general prevention claim.

review.summary: COVID-OUT reported fewer later clinician diagnoses of long COVID in participants assigned metformin during their acute infection. Its result belongs to prevention, because treatment began before the long-term illness being counted. A reader who already has long COVID faces a different question, and this study cannot supply that answer. Our interpretation is that the finding deserves attention without becoming a general endorsement of metformin. The clinical meaning depends on who entered the study, how a diagnosis was counted, and what later trials found. This draft preserves those boundaries and does not assign an evidence grade or recommend a regimen.
review.methods: The trial used masked random allocation and a factorial design, allowing metformin and matched placebo groups to contain balanced co-treatments. The long-term analysis included 1126 people, while the original randomized population was larger. Those counts answer different questions: assignment describes the trial population, whereas the long-term group describes the participants contributing to this analysis. Eligibility selected adults with overweight or obesity and a recent infection, without a known earlier infection. Our appraisal priority is therefore both internal comparison and applicability. Neither randomization nor a large initial recruitment total automatically makes the result representative of people with different clinical histories.
review.results: By day 300, estimated cumulative incidence was 6.3% with metformin and 10.4% with placebo; the reported hazard ratio was 0.59 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.39 to 0.89. These are time-to-event estimates, not instructions to divide an invented event count by the enrollment total. The direction favors metformin for the measured diagnosis outcome. Our interpretation remains narrower than a claim that every long COVID symptom was prevented. A diagnosis depends on recognition and contact with care, and the study's endpoint does not directly measure every possible symptom experience. Outcome definitions need to travel with the number whenever it is quoted.
review.limits: Long-term diagnosis was a secondary outcome added during the trial, and participation in extended follow-up was selective. The paper itself says it does not establish treatment benefit in people who already have long COVID. A correction notice is linked to the paper, but this pilot has not reconciled its exact amended text. The acquired manuscript also gives a different placebo percentage in its Discussion than in its Results. We use the Results figure provisionally and keep publication on hold. This is a source-integrity question for the review packet, not a reason to silently choose whichever number makes the claim sound stronger.
review.sources: The original report, trial identifier NCT04510194, and linked correction remain the source trail for this draft. The source file is an HTML manuscript acquired from PMC; no PDF was downloaded or visually audited for this record. Supplemental materials and the acute-outcome companion report require further reconciliation before a complete trial-family appraisal. Funding and author disclosures are recorded separately from the result because they inform scrutiny but do not determine whether an estimate is true. The next editorial step is an exact-version source audit followed by independent human review. This preview is not that approval and should not be presented as a released appraisal.

sources.title: Metformin on the Presence of COVID-19 Symptoms 6 Months after Infection: The ACTIV-6 Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: Accelerating COVID-19 Therapeutic Interventions and Vaccines (ACTIV)-6 Study Group and Investigators
sources.design: Quadruple-blind randomized decentralized placebo-controlled platform trial
sources.population: Outpatients at least 30 years old with acute COVID; prior infection/vaccination allowed
sources.preview: This newer randomized prevention trial did not meet its efficacy threshold for symptoms at six months. A secondary clinician-diagnosis outcome suggested benefit, but it should not replace the primary result. The study had few observed events and missing follow-up responses. These findings concern treatment during acute infection, not starting metformin to treat an established long COVID illness.

review.summary: ACTIV-6 tested metformin begun during acute infection and did not meet its stated efficacy threshold for symptoms attributed to COVID-19 at six months. A secondary outcome, participant-reported clinician diagnosis of long COVID, pointed toward benefit. These findings should be read together without swapping their roles. Our interpretation is that the primary result limits the strength of a broad prevention claim, while the secondary finding remains relevant to future investigation. The trial does not test whether metformin treats symptoms in someone who already has long COVID. Keeping that distinction visible makes the evidence useful even when it does not give a simple yes or no.
review.methods: The modified intention-to-treat analysis included 2983 adults from a later pandemic period, and prior infection or vaccination was common. The study compared a 14-day metformin course with matched placebo during acute illness. Its primary long-term outcome asked about symptoms on a particular follow-up day rather than accumulating all clinician diagnoses over ten months. Our reading treats this difference as part of the scientific question, not a nuisance to erase. A result can differ from an earlier trial because the people, background risk, timing, measurement, or actual treatment effect differs. This pilot does not attempt to separate those explanations quantitatively.
review.results: The adjusted symptom risk difference at day 180 was −0.8 percentage points, with a 95% credible interval from −2.2 to 0.6. The posterior probability of benefit was 0.83, below the trial's 0.975 threshold. A negative difference favors metformin, but the interval also contains no difference and a small difference in the other direction. Our interpretation is therefore uncertainty about the size and presence of benefit under this study's model, rather than proof of equal outcomes. The favorable secondary diagnosis result does not override the primary finding. Its intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it needs its own cautious, outcome-specific reading.
review.limits: The day-180 symptom outcome was missing for 593 participants, and observed events were uncommon. The article reports changes to the analysis plan after the day-28 analysis, including the efficacy threshold and provisions for fewer events. These choices require protocol and statistical-plan comparison in a formal appraisal. Missing responses were handled through a model, which is more informative than pretending every missing person was symptom-free but still depends on assumptions. Tolerability was not comprehensively assessed beyond selected safety events. We therefore do not turn the paper's reassuring safety language into a general safety rating, especially for people outside its eligibility and clinical context.
review.sources: The current journal report and its NCBI identity are linked, and the earlier preprint is treated as another version of the same report rather than a separate replication. Relevant publisher HTML sections were accessible through the research tool, while direct HTML download returned an access error. A saved extraction snapshot supports the located findings; it is not a full downloaded PDF. The supplement, protocol changes, and comprehensive conflict disclosures remain review tasks. Our priority before release is to resolve those tasks and obtain human approval of the exact content version. Neither a successful import nor this written explanation is a completed risk-of-bias assessment.

sources.title: Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir and Symptoms in Adults With Postacute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 Infection: The STOP-PASC Randomized Clinical Trial
sources.population: Adults with at least two moderate/severe core PASC symptoms, at least 3 months duration
sources.preview: A 15-day nirmatrelvir–ritonavir course did not significantly improve the selected symptom outcomes in STOP-PASC. Participants already had long COVID, so the question differed from acute treatment or prevention. Symptoms improved in both groups. The small, selected, single-center population limits broader conclusions, and later trials still require full-text reconciliation. The source includes a correction to Figure 2.

review.summary: STOP-PASC did not find a significant benefit from a 15-day nirmatrelvir–ritonavir course for its selected long COVID symptoms. The study is relevant to established illness because participants already had persistent symptoms when treatment began. Both groups improved over time, which makes the randomized comparison more informative than a before-and-after story about the active drug alone. Our interpretation is that this regimen did not demonstrate the expected advantage in the enrolled population. The finding does not settle every antiviral, duration, symptom subtype, or possible mechanism. It does challenge a claim that improvement after taking this treatment, by itself, proves a drug effect.
review.methods: Researchers randomized 155 adults at Stanford to nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir or placebo plus ritonavir. The primary assessment pooled severity across six core symptom groups at ten weeks. Enrollment stopped early after the prespecified futility criterion was reached. This design matters because the control was not simply an inert substitute for every component of the active combination. Our reading keeps the exact comparator in every interpretation. The trial also selected participants according to clinical and medication criteria, so its experience should not be extended to excluded people without further evidence. Randomization supports comparison within the trial; it does not eliminate every question about applicability.
review.results: The primary pooled symptom comparison did not show a significant between-group difference. As an illustrative secondary outcome, the adjusted difference in PROMIS fatigue change was 0.38 points, with a 95% confidence interval from −2.40 to 3.15. Fatigue improved within both groups, but that is not the same as evidence that the active treatment caused greater improvement. Our interpretation gives priority to the comparison the trial was designed to make. The interval also prevents a claim that an exact zero effect has been established. Secondary and exploratory findings need caution because multiple comparisons can generate apparently interesting differences even without a reproducible treatment advantage.
review.limits: This was a single-center study, with a smaller sample than planned and a mostly vaccinated population with prolonged symptoms. Taste disturbance differed between groups and could have affected masking of self-reported outcomes. Adverse events and treatment discontinuations were recorded, but a modest trial cannot provide a complete picture of rare harms or risks in excluded patients. Our review therefore keeps harms visible alongside the absence of demonstrated benefit. It also separates study exclusions from medical contraindications: the latter require current product-specific authoritative information and qualified clinical interpretation. There is no dosing recommendation in this review and no inference that a longer course would work.
review.sources: The PMC article includes a correction dated July 22, 2024, concerning the placement of dashed lines in Figure 2. We retain that notice with the paper rather than treating the corrected figure as a new study. The source was acquired as HTML; its tables were read as text, and PDF visual verification remains pending. Pfizer funded the trial and collaborated on its design, execution, and manuscript review, with disclosures recorded in the evidence data. Later nirmatrelvir–ritonavir trials have been identified, including RECOVER-VITAL, but full-text reconciliation remains incomplete. This draft is an original reading aid awaiting source audit and human editorial approval, not a released clinical recommendation.

guides.title: Metformin and long COVID prevention
guides.description: Two trials ask whether treatment during acute infection changes later outcomes.

sections.label: Answer
sections.title: Does metformin prevent long COVID?
sections.paragraph: The selected randomized evidence gives a promising but unsettled answer for metformin started during acute infection. COVID-OUT reported fewer later clinician diagnoses, whereas the newer ACTIV-6 trial did not meet its efficacy threshold for the primary symptom outcome. These trials used different populations and different ways of counting long COVID, so their headline results should not be treated as interchangeable replications. The current draft supports examining the exact question before interpreting any prevention claim.

The current draft supports examining the exact question before interpreting any prevention claim.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Prevention is a different question from treatment
sections.paragraph: Both prevention trials began medication during acute COVID-19, before the later outcome was assessed. Neither trial answers whether starting the same medicine months later reverses an established long COVID illness. This distinction is central to interpreting a repurposing claim because the same molecule can be tested at different disease stages for different purposes. A reader considering an established-illness question should follow the treatment evidence separately instead of borrowing a prevention result.

sections.paragraph: In ACTIV-6, the estimated difference in day-180 symptom risk favored metformin by 0.8 percentage points, but the credible interval included both benefit and no benefit. Its secondary clinician-diagnosis outcome gave a more favorable signal than the primary symptom outcome. Our interpretation is that a statement about diagnosis cannot stand in for a statement about all persistent symptoms. The outcome hierarchy, uncertainty, and missing responses should remain attached to the result wherever it is summarized.

guides.description: Prevention results do not establish benefit after symptoms are already persistent.

sections.label: Answer
sections.title: Has treatment benefit been demonstrated?
sections.paragraph: The acquired abstract of a South Korean randomized trial did not demonstrate improved recovery from established long COVID after a short metformin course. That is direct treatment evidence, unlike studies that started medication during acute infection to prevent later illness. It does not establish that every duration or patient subgroup would have the same outcome. This page is intentionally provisional because the full report and other current treatment records still need reconciliation before a complete treatment synthesis.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Read what recovery meant in the trial
sections.paragraph: The Korean trial defined recovery using a threshold on a PASC symptom index at follow-up. Its definition tells the reader which change counted as an event and prevents an overly broad reading of the word recovery. A threshold crossing should not silently become a claim that every symptom disappeared or that normal function was restored. The primary abstract supplies the trial's operational definition, but instrument details, attrition, and clinically meaningful change still need full-text inspection.

sections.title: The comparison matters more than improvement alone
sections.paragraph: The abstract reports recovery in both the metformin group and the placebo group, without a significant advantage for metformin. Improvement within a treated group is therefore insufficient to attribute that improvement to the medicine. Our reading focuses on the randomized comparison and keeps the reported treatment duration attached to the conclusion. A complete assessment must inspect the analysis population, missing outcomes, and uncertainty around between-group differences instead of relying on an attractive before-and-after change.

sections.label: Answer
sections.title: What did the trials find?
sections.paragraph: STOP-PASC did not demonstrate a significant improvement in its selected long COVID symptom outcomes after an extended nirmatrelvir–ritonavir course. The newer RECOVER-VITAL abstract also reports no significant primary-outcome benefit across its studied symptom phenotypes. This selected evidence challenges a broad claim that an extended course reliably treats established long COVID. context.text: A registry, preprint, published report and follow-up can describe one study.
They are related sources, not independent replications.

glossary.title: Randomization
glossary.meaning: Assigning trial participants to groups by chance.
glossary.context: Chance assignment supports a fairer comparison because neither the participant nor researcher chooses the treatment group. It does not, by itself, solve missing-data or outcome-measurement problems.
glossary.examples: STOP-PASC assigned participants between nirmatrelvir–ritonavir and placebo–ritonavir, preserving a specific treatment comparison.

glossary.title: Absolute risk
glossary.meaning: The chance of a defined event occurring over a specified period.
glossary.context: It is different from the ratio of risks between two groups. The event definition and follow-up time belong with the number.
glossary.examples: An absolute risk difference expressed in percentage points should not be relabeled as a relative percentage reduction. The ACTIV-6 primary estimate uses percentage points.

glossary.title: Off-label use
glossary.meaning: Use of an approved drug in a way not included in its approved labeling.
glossary.context: The FDA explains that this can involve a different condition, route or dose. It does not mean that the FDA has established safety and effectiveness for that unapproved use.
glossary.examples: A regulatory assessment must name the product, jurisdiction, indication and date. This glossary definition does not establish the current status of any specific drug–long-COVID use.
